summary: Premier Smith says Alberta stays in Canada with no second separation vote, while early counts show most immigration questions passing narrowly. A U.S. importer has sued over the 50% tariffs.
body: Alberta's referendum is still the main story. In a televised address Tuesday evening, Premier Danielle Smith said Albertans had "made their choice" and that she will not hold another separation referendum while she is premier [^1][^2]. She acknowledged "legitimate frustrations" with Ottawa but said disputes should go through political and legal channels [^1]. Prime Minister Mark Carney's office issued a statement saying "Albertans chose Canada" and focused on trade and building projects [^5]. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was "thrilled" with the result and called for new pipelines [^2].

The other nine questions are closer. In unofficial counts on Tuesday, yes was ahead on all five immigration questions, mostly at about 54 to 58 per cent. Requiring proof of citizenship to vote had roughly two-thirds support [^1][^3]. On the four constitutional questions (changes to Canada's basic legal rulebook), yes led narrowly on three. The exception was letting Alberta opt out of federal programs without losing federal money, which was trailing at about 51 per cent no [^1][^3]. Edmonton voted no on all nine [^1]. These results are non-binding, meaning they guide the government but do not force it to act. Official results are expected Oct. 29 [^3]. Carney said immigration disputes can be settled without changing the Constitution [^1]. Ottawa's updated immigration plan is due in November [^4]. My read: these questions set up negotiations with Ottawa rather than immediate changes.

On trade, a U.S. food importer filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. Court of International Trade. It challenges the 50 per cent tariffs (taxes on imports) on about $20 billion US of Canadian goods. Those tariffs took effect Aug. 22 [^6][^7]. The suit argues President Donald Trump went beyond his authority under a 1930 law and asks for the tariffs to be blocked and refunded [^6][^7]. Otherwise it was a quiet day for economic news, with no major data releases. The Bank of Canada's interest rate decision is still set for Oct. 28.
differences: Reactions to the vote differ. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre backed Smith's push for more provincial say on immigration. Separatist organizer Jeff Rath said he would seek a UCP meeting to remove Smith. Avnish Nanda, who campaigned against the immigration questions, cited polls suggesting some voters were confused by the wording. Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi called the referendum a mistake [^1][^2].

reads.title: Albertans mixed on other referendum questions after rejecting separation
reads.summary: A plain explainer of each of the nine non-separation questions, covering immigration, voter ID, judges, the Senate and federal programs, with Tuesday's unofficial results.
